Arthur’s boots crunched over calcified barnacles. The storm had vomited a feast of debris: shredded jellyfish, blackened driftwood, a single, salt-stiffened boot. He spotted a glint nestled in a tangle of bladderwrack. It wasn't glass, but a heavy, amber-colored resin vessel, shaped like a teardrop.

He knelt, his joints grinding like shifting shale. He pried it from the grit. The resin was warm, unnervingly so, as if it had retained a feverish heat from some deep-sea vent. Inside, a sliver of vellum sat coiled, a dark, curled spine. There was no ink visible through the amber, only a shadow that looked less like writing and more like a bruise.

Arthur wiped the brine from his spectacles. He didn't use a knife; he used a thumbnail to crack the seal of dried salt. As the resin split, the scent hit him—not ozone, but scorched cinnamon and old copper. He unrolled the vellum. The script didn't sit on the page; it bled into the fibers, violet and frantic, spelling words that made the lighthouse beam feel suddenly, terrifyingly dim.
